specPoints.text: understand how ions are formed by electron loss or gain
draw dot-and-cross diagrams to show the formation of ionic compounds by electron transfer, limited to combinations of elements from Groups 1, 2, 3 and 5, 6, 7 only outer electrons need be shown

primer.text: From Ionic Bonding you already know that metal atoms lose their outer electrons and non-metal atoms gain them, forming ions with full outer shells. This note shows how that electron transfer is drawn: dot-and-cross diagrams that make the movement of electrons, and the charges left behind, visible on the page.

lessons.title: Sodium chloride dot and cross diagram
sourceHeadings: Dot and cross diagrams for ionic compounds
Sodium chloride dot and cross diagram
lessons.opening: A dot-and-cross diagram draws the outer electrons of each atom, using a different symbol for each atom involved. When a metal reacts with a non-metal, electrons move across from the metal to the non-metal, and square brackets around each ion carry its charge. Sodium chloride is the standard example: one electron passes from sodium to chlorine.
keyPoints: In a dot-and-cross diagram each atom's outer electrons get their own symbol, dots for one atom and crosses for the other.
Sodium is a Group 1 metal, so it loses its single outer electron to reach a full outer shell.
Chlorine is a Group 7 non-metal, so it gains that electron to complete its own outer shell.
The transfer produces a 1+ sodium ion and a 1- chloride ion, giving the formula NaCl.
Large square brackets enclose each ion, with the charge written outside at the top right in superscript.

low.restatement: Draw one atom's outer electrons as dots and the other atom's as crosses. Sodium hands its one outer electron over to chlorine, both end with full outer shells, and the finished picture shows a 1+ and a 1- ion inside brackets as NaCl.
low.analogy: Picture two students keeping record cards: one card marks each electron with a dot, the other with a cross, so after the handover you can see exactly which electron came from whom.
low.examPointer: Only the outer shells are drawn; inner shells earn no credit, so keep the diagram to the outermost electrons and label both ion charges.

medium.restatement: The diagram is a bookkeeping device for electron transfer: dots mark the metal's outer electrons and crosses the non-metal's, so the moved electrons stay identifiable. After the handover both ions show full outer shells, sodium has lost one electron to sit at 1+, and chlorine has gained one to sit at 1-.
medium.analogy: Think of labelled coins in two jars: each coin keeps its marking when it moves jar, so anyone can audit later which coins migrated and how many each jar now holds.
medium.examPointer: Marks sit on three details: different symbols per atom, outer shells only, and charges outside the brackets; omit any one and the diagram scores partially.

check.stem: In the sodium chloride dot-and-cross diagram, how many electrons are transferred from the sodium atom to the chlorine atom?

options.text: One
options.explanation: Sodium is in Group 1 with a single outer electron, and one electron completes chlorine's outer shell.

options.text: Two
options.explanation: Two transfers would suit a Group 2 metal such as magnesium; sodium carries only one outer electron.

options.text: Seven
options.explanation: Seven is the count chlorine already has; it receives one electron rather than giving seven away.
options.misconception: outer-electron count confused with transfer count

options.text: None, the electrons are shared
options.explanation: Sharing belongs to covalent bonding; sodium chloride forms by full transfer between a metal and a non-metal.
options.misconception: covalent sharing model applied to ionic bonding

check.stem: Where is the charge written on each ion in a finished dot-and-cross diagram?

options.text: Outside the square brackets, at the top right, as a superscript
options.explanation: The brackets enclose the ion and its electrons, and the charge sits outside them at the top right.

options.text: Inside the square brackets, next to the nucleus
options.explanation: Charges describe the whole ion, not the nucleus alone, so they sit outside the brackets.

options.text: Underneath the ion, on a separate line
options.explanation: Convention places the charge at the top right; a separate line is not the accepted layout.

options.text: Charges are not written on dot-and-cross diagrams
options.explanation: The charge is essential information on an ionic diagram; omitting it loses the mark.

check.stem: Why does the chlorine atom in the diagram end with a 1- charge?

options.text: Because it has gained one electron, giving it one more electron than protons
options.explanation: The extra transferred electron tips the balance from neutral to 1-.

options.text: Because it has lost one electron
options.explanation: Losing electrons gives positive charges; chlorine gains the transferred electron.

options.text: Because it shares an electron with sodium
options.explanation: No sharing happens in ionic bonding; the electron transfers completely to the chlorine.

options.text: Because chlorine atoms always carry a charge
options.explanation: A chlorine atom starts neutral; the charge appears only after the transfer.

check.stem: Magnesium oxide forms from magnesium and oxygen. How many electrons move in total?

options.text: Two, both from magnesium to oxygen
options.explanation: Magnesium is in Group 2 and oxygen in Group 6, so two electrons transfer and both ions reach full outer shells.

options.text: One
options.explanation: One electron would leave magnesium at 1+ and oxygen at 1-, charges that do not match their groups.

options.text: Two, one travelling in each direction
options.explanation: Both transferred electrons come from magnesium; oxygen gains rather than trades electrons.

options.text: Four
options.explanation: Four electrons would mean two complete transfers twice over; the group numbers fix the count at two.

check.stem: Which combinations must you be able to draw ionic dot-and-cross diagrams for in this course?

options.text: Combinations of elements from Groups 1, 2 and 3 with elements from Groups 5, 6 and 7
options.explanation: The spec limits ionic dot-and-cross diagrams to those group pairings, with only outer electrons shown.

options.text: Every element in the Periodic Table paired with every other
options.explanation: The requirement is limited to the listed groups; wider pairings are beyond the spec.

options.text: Only sodium chloride and magnesium oxide
options.explanation: These are the worked examples, not the limit; any pairing from the listed groups can be asked.
options.misconception: examples mistaken for the full scope

options.text: Transition metals paired with halogens
options.explanation: Transition metals sit outside the listed groups for this diagram type.

lessons.title: Magnesium oxide dot and cross diagram
sourceHeadings: Magnesium oxide dot and cross diagram
lessons.opening: The magnesium oxide diagram repeats the sodium chloride story with two electrons instead of one. Magnesium, in Group 2, gives away both of its outer electrons; oxygen, in Group 6, receives both and completes its outer shell. The finished diagram shows a 2+ ion and a 2- ion in brackets, and the charges cancel to give the formula MgO.
keyPoints: Magnesium sits in Group 2, so a magnesium atom has two outer electrons to give away.
Oxygen sits in Group 6, so an oxygen atom needs two more electrons to complete its outer shell.
Both transferred electrons come from the magnesium atom, and both are received by the oxygen atom.
The ions formed are Mg2+ and O2-, and the formula of magnesium oxide is MgO.
The diagram needs only the outer shells drawn, with dots and crosses distinguishing the two atoms.

low.restatement: Magnesium's two outer electrons transfer to one oxygen atom. Draw the two dots crossing over as crosses, bracket both ions, and mark them 2+ and 2-; the charges cancel one-to-one, which is why the formula reads MgO.
low.analogy: It is like paying a two-coin fare in one transaction: the buyer hands over both coins together, the payment completes exactly, and the receipt shows a single two-coin handover.
low.examPointer: State the group numbers when you explain the diagram; the marks reward linking Group 2 and Group 6 to the two-electron transfer.

medium.restatement: The 2+ and 2- charges arise directly from the group positions: a Group 2 atom empties its outer shell while a Group 6 atom tops up by the same count. Because the two electrons move together to a single oxygen atom, the ion ratio stays one-to-one and the formula is MgO.
medium.analogy: Picture a shop that only accepts exact payment in two coins: the buyer hands over both at once, the seller's account completes, and the record shows a single two-coin transfer.
medium.examPointer: For any Group 2 with Group 6 pairing the same two-electron transfer applies, so practise spotting the pattern rather than relearning each case.

check.stem: What charge does the oxide ion carry in the magnesium oxide diagram, and why?

options.text: 2-, because it gains two electrons
options.explanation: Two extra electrons give the oxide ion two more negatives than positives.

options.text: 1-, because only one shell is involved
options.explanation: Shell count sets nothing here; the charge follows the two electrons gained.
options.misconception: shell count linked to charge size

options.text: 2+, because it lost two protons
options.explanation: Protons never transfer during bonding; oxygen gains electrons, so its charge is negative.

options.text: 6-, because oxygen is in Group 6
options.explanation: The group number counts outer electrons, not the charge; oxygen gains only two.
options.misconception: group number read as the charge

check.stem: In the diagram, how are the two transferred electrons shown?

options.text: They keep the magnesium atom's symbol and appear inside the oxide ion's brackets
options.explanation: Each electron keeps the symbol of the atom it came from, so the transferred pair shows the donor inside the acceptor's shell.

options.text: They are redrawn with the oxygen atom's symbol
options.explanation: Changing the symbol would hide where the electrons came from; the donor's marking travels with them.

options.text: They are left out, since transferred electrons cannot be drawn
options.explanation: The transferred electrons are exactly what the diagram must show; leaving them out would hide the transfer.

options.text: They sit between the two ions as a shared pair
options.explanation: A shared pair would depict covalent bonding; here the electrons belong wholly to the oxide ion.

check.stem: Why is the formula of magnesium oxide MgO rather than Mg2O2?

options.text: Because the 2+ and 2- charges cancel one-to-one, so the simplest ratio needs one of each ion
options.explanation: The charges are equal and opposite, and formulas give the simplest whole-number ratio.

options.text: Because magnesium oxide is a molecular compound
options.explanation: Magnesium oxide is ionic with a giant lattice; the ratio reflects the lattice's repeating unit.

options.text: Because the number 2 is never written in a formula
options.explanation: Counts of 2 appear whenever the charges demand them, as in CaCl2; the one-to-one ratio here needs no 2.

options.text: Because oxygen cannot sit next to two magnesium ions
options.explanation: In the lattice each oxide ion does sit among several magnesium ions; the formula simply reports the simplest ratio.
options.misconception: lattice geometry confused with the formula ratio

check.stem: Which detail of a correct ionic dot-and-cross diagram does the exam expect?

options.text: Square brackets around both ions with the charges written outside
options.explanation: The brackets and external charges show that the products are separate ions, not one shared structure.

options.text: Arrows showing the electrons orbiting between the ions
options.explanation: Once transferred, the electrons belong to one ion; orbiting arrows are not part of the convention.

options.text: All electron shells, inner and outer, fully drawn
options.explanation: Only the outer electrons need be shown, as the spec states.

options.text: A shared box around both ions instead of separate brackets
options.explanation: The ions are distinct charged particles, each with its own brackets and charge.

check.stem: How does the magnesium oxide transfer differ from the sodium chloride transfer?

options.text: Two electrons transfer instead of one, giving charges of 2+ and 2- rather than 1+ and 1-
options.explanation: The group positions of the two metals set the transfer counts: Group 2 loses two, Group 1 loses one.

options.text: Electrons move from the non-metal to the metal
options.explanation: In both compounds the metal provides the electrons and the non-metal receives them.

options.text: The electrons are shared in pairs rather than transferred
options.explanation: Both compounds are ionic; sharing belongs to the covalent notes that follow.

options.text: Nothing differs, as both diagrams show one electron moving
options.explanation: The chloride diagram shows one electron transferring, while the oxide diagram shows two.

glossary.definition: A drawing that uses a different symbol for each atom's outer electrons to show how they are transferred or shared.
An electron in the outermost occupied shell of an atom; only these are drawn in the diagrams of this note.
A charged particle formed when an atom loses or gains electrons.
One of the fixed positions around the nucleus that electrons occupy; the outermost one is completed by transfer here.
